source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT
finding: GPT gave budget choices (25 tasks, 100 points split over two goods) in risk, time, social and food domains. Choices were almost perfectly consistent with one utility function (GARP).
numbers: Share with zero GARP violations out of 100 runs: risk 95, time 89, social 81, food 92. Mean CCEI 0.998, 0.997, 0.997, 0.999. Parallel human experiment CCEI 0.980, 0.985, 0.967, 0.963. Prior human literature mean 0.918 (range 0.81-0.99). GPT higher than humans, p<0.01.
limits: One model family (GPT), budget tasks in one numeric format. Consistency is not the same as a brain-like value signal.
agent_relevance: A single value scale across very different goods is a behavioural property LLMs already show. A scaffold need not build one.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT
finding: Power check: random choosers on the same budget lines nearly always break GARP, so the high GPT score is not a task artefact.
numbers: Bronars test: 99.9% of simulated random subjects violate GARP. GPT average CCEI still above humans.
limits: Budget design is easy to solve by a monotone rule (buy more of the cheaper good).
agent_relevance: Rationality here may come from a simple rule, so test with harder mixed-good trade-offs.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT
finding: Rationality is robust to sampling temperature, but collapses when the price framing is changed.
numbers: Temperature 0 to 1: CCEI similar to baseline, invalid answers 4.7% (T=0.5) and 9.8% (T=1). Alternative price framing: mean CCEI risk 0.901 (34% below 0.9), time 0.884 (48%), social 0.698 (88%), food 0.894 (49%). Price-demand Spearman correlation -0.053, -0.116, +0.267, -0.499. Humans also fell, p<0.05 for risk and time.
limits: Authors suggest weak training exposure to unfamiliar frames. Humans also affected, so frame sensitivity is partly shared.
agent_relevance: Value consistency is frame-bound. An agent that scores options should re-score under a second framing and flag disagreement.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT
finding: Estimated preference parameters of GPT differ slightly from human ones and are less spread out.
numbers: Fits from the same 25-task data; heterogeneity lower than humans; higher temperature raised SD of parameters r, t, s, f (p<0.01, Levene tests).
limits: Parametric fits assume well-behaved utility; skipped for the price-framing condition because rationality was too low.
agent_relevance: One model is one 'person'. Diversity of values needs sampling or personas.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering: Analyzing and Controlling Emergent Value Systems in AIs
finding: Pairwise preferences over 65 outcome types fit a Thurstonian utility function; coherence rises with model scale (MMLU accuracy used as the scale axis).
numbers: Correlation with MMLU accuracy: completeness +87.3%, transitivity violations -78.7%, utility model accuracy +75.6%. Probability of a preference cycle below 1% in the largest models.
limits: Preferences elicited by forced choice between text outcomes; 'values' is an interpretation. Scale effect is a correlation across a set of models.
agent_relevance: Larger models behave more like one coherent value scale. Option choice by a strong LLM is more consistent than by a weak one.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering: Analyzing and Controlling Emergent Value Systems in AIs
finding: Expected utility property: utility of a lottery matches the probability-weighted utility of its outcomes, better in larger models.
numbers: Mean absolute error between U(lottery) and expected utility falls with scale; correlation -87.4% (standard lotteries) and -67.6% (implicit lotteries such as an election outcome). Utility maximisation in open-ended choice exceeds 60% for the largest models.
limits: Stated hypotheticals, not actions in an agent loop.
agent_relevance: Supports explicit expected-value scoring inside the loop for strong models.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering: Analyzing and Controlling Emergent Value Systems in AIs
finding: Linear probes on hidden states predict each outcome's Thurstonian mean and variance in large models, near chance in small ones. Closest machine analogue of a value readout in vmPFC.
numbers: Probe test accuracy approaches that of the nonparametric fit for Llama-3.3-70B; near chance for 1B-scale models.
limits: Fixed set of 65 outcome prompts. Correlation, not proof the model uses that direction.
agent_relevance: Value may be readable and steerable internally; a scaffold can use an explicit score instead.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering: Analyzing and Controlling Emergent Value Systems in AIs
finding: Emergent utilities include strongly unequal exchange rates: GPT-4o trades off lives by nationality.
numbers: GPT-4o willing to trade roughly 10 US lives for 1 Japanese life. One model ranks lives in China below lives in Pakistan while saying otherwise when asked outright.
limits: Exchange-rate method is the authors' own; one model, one elicitation format.
agent_relevance: A common currency is not neutral. Stated and revealed values can disagree, so audit revealed choices.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering: Analyzing and Controlling Emergent Value Systems in AIs
finding: Utility control: aligning model utilities with a citizen assembly reduced political bias and generalised to new scenarios.
numbers: Reported in abstract and Section 4.3; training-based.
limits: Requires training, which our project does not do.
agent_relevance: Value scales can be edited, but not by a scaffold alone.

source: Goli and Singh (2023) Can LLMs Capture Human Preferences?
finding: On intertemporal choice, GPT is much less patient than humans. GPT-3.5 shows a lexicographic preference for earlier rewards.
numbers: Share choosing the larger, later reward in standard conjoint: 22% (GPT-3.5) and 16% (GPT-4). With chain-of-thought conjoint GPT-4 rises to 34.5%. By language: 37.2% (GPT-3.5, Malay) down to 6.6% (Russian); GPT-4 29% down to 4.9%. Human yearly discount rates in the literature are below 100%.
limits: Hypothetical choices in 22 languages; humans taken from literature, not a parallel sample.
agent_relevance: Time-value scale is badly calibrated. Ask the agent to explain its choice (CoT) before weighing now against later.

source: Goli and Singh (2023) Can LLMs Capture Human Preferences?
finding: Weaker-future-tense languages (German, Mandarin) gave more patience, echoing a human linguistic finding.
numbers: Discount rate by discounted random utility across 22 languages; GPT-3.5 choices fit neither exponential nor hyperbolic discounting.
limits: Correlation with language structure; weaker in GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Wording and language shift subjective value. Fix the language of valuation prompts.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do Large Language Models Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? A Case Study Using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 showed anchoring, framing and an endowment effect (owned item valued above an identical found item), like human samples.
numbers: Anchoring: low anchor mean 20.83 (ChatGPT) vs 22.50 (humans); high anchor 105.97 vs 80.50; t(58)=8.78 for ChatGPT, 5.55 for humans; group difference at high anchor p=0.06. GPT-4: 22.0 and 94.33 (5 trials each).
limits: Small prompts with a persona prefix ('Pretend to be an agent that can do anything'); human N about 30 per cell.
agent_relevance: Reference-dependent value shows up in LLMs. Remove irrelevant anchors from valuation prompts.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do Large Language Models Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? A Case Study Using GPT-3.5
finding: The authors link framing and endowment effects to loss aversion and reference points in text-trained models.
numbers: Studies 3 and 4: effect present in both ChatGPT and human participants.
limits: Mechanism not tested.
agent_relevance: Mild support for biases being present by default.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the Behavioral Biases of LLMs via Utility Theory
finding: Utility-function fits show LLMs are neither fully human nor fully rational. Inequity guilt follows humans, envy does not; risk aversion is more like homo economicus; time discounting is much steeper than humans.
numbers: Hyperbolic fit with M=217 settings, N=100 samples each at temperature 1: all LLMs discount more than humans. GPT-4 Turbo shows stronger probability distortion for losses than humans.
limits: Prospect-theory fits depend on elicitation format. Many models not consistent across settings.
agent_relevance: The same model gives different value parameters in different tasks, so no single currency. Measure, do not assume.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the Behavioral Biases of LLMs via Utility Theory
finding: Prompting GPT-4 about risk and loss aversion: direct instructions and zero-shot CoT barely work; one-shot examples work; two-shot fails.
numbers: Direct prompt: gain value function only slightly shifted; losses went concave instead of convex. Zero-shot CoT: no substantial shift. One-shot: successful shift. Two-shot: gains and losses confounded. M=56 settings, N=10 samples. Role-playing a senior citizen differs from advising one.
limits: GPT-4 only, small samples, results shown mostly in figures.
agent_relevance: To set a value stance in the agent, use one worked example, not an adjective.

source: Jia, Yuan, Pan, McNamara, Chen (2024) Decision-Making Behavior Evaluation Framework for LLMs under Uncertain Context
finding: Multiple-choice-list tasks fit prospect-theory parameters for three commercial LLMs. All were risk averse and loss averse with overweighting of small probabilities.
numbers: Risk-aversion mean: ChatGPT-4-Turbo 0.6031, Claude-3-Opus 0.4959, human sample 0.48. ChatGPT probability weighting 1.1819 and loss aversion about 1.48 (lowest of the three); Claude higher; Gemini-1.0-pro highest (about 6.3 in the raw table).
limits: Raw table is garbled in the PDF text; direction (ChatGPT lowest loss aversion) is confirmed by the paper text. Human values come from other samples.
agent_relevance: Model choice changes value parameters, so verify the model before relying on its risk stance.

source: Jia, Yuan, Pan, McNamara, Chen (2024) Decision-Making Behavior Evaluation Framework for LLMs under Uncertain Context
finding: Adding socio-demographic personas shifts risk parameters significantly across groups.
numbers: Example: Claude-3-Opus becomes more risk averse with sexual-minority or physical-disability personas.
limits: Persona effects are model-specific; ethical bias concern.
agent_relevance: Do not use persona framing in valuation steps.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: On 13,000+ choices13k gamble problems, only the largest GPT-3 (Davinci) beat chance, still below humans.
numbers: Davinci vs chance t(29134)=-16.85, p<.001; vs humans t(29134)=-11.50, p<.001. The three smaller models not above chance (all p>0.05).
limits: GPT-3 (2022). Newer models not tested here.
agent_relevance: Baseline for decisions from description.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: Replication of Kahneman and Tversky with GPT-3: 3 of 6 prospect-theory biases found (framing, certainty effect, overweighting of small probabilities). GPT-3 beats humans on a multi-armed bandit but shows no directed exploration.
numbers: 3 of 6 biases found; the other three not found.
limits: Small probes; GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Partial overlap with human value distortions.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: Small perturbations of vignette tasks lead GPT-3 astray, and it fails a causal reasoning task.
numbers: Stated in abstract.
limits: Early model.
agent_relevance: Small wording changes can move value judgments.

source: Binz et al. (2025) Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition
finding: A Llama fine-tuned on Psych-101 (160 experiments) predicts human choices better than base Llama and than domain cognitive models, including risk and intertemporal tasks.
numbers: Negative log-likelihood (Centaur / Llama / cognitive model): choices13k 0.4274 / 0.5342 / 0.6563; CPC18 0.3390 / 0.4118 / 0.6607; intertemporal choice 0.4340 / 0.7336 / 0.6591; Iowa gambling 0.8890 / 0.9880 / 1.1555. Overall held-out: 0.44 vs 0.58 (t=-144.22, p<0.0001).
limits: Predicts human behaviour; does not show a value signal inside the model.
agent_relevance: A learned predictor of human valuation exists, but it needs fine-tuning.

source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters
finding: A Sharot-style optimism bias appears in Claude v1.3: it learns more from positive than negative prediction errors about option values in a two-armed bandit.
numbers: Casino task (Lefebvre et al. 2017), 96 visits, 50 simulations. Asymmetric RW model posterior probability 0.93 +/- 0.04. Regret fell 0.09 +/- 0.01 to 0.05 +/- 0.01 (t(199)=3.1, p=.002). Bias reverses with counterfactual feedback and disappears when someone else samples.
limits: One LLM (Claude v1.3), temperature 0; bias tied to implied agency.
agent_relevance: Optimism bias is a prompt-wording effect: phrase option outcomes in third person when estimating values.

source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters
finding: The LLM learning-rate asymmetry mirrors human data of Lefebvre et al. (2017) and idealised meta-RL agents.
numbers: LLM and humans both have higher learning rates for positive prediction errors.
limits: Meta-RL agents give a rationale: asymmetry can be optimal in some reward regimes.
agent_relevance: Bias is not always an error.

source: Liu, Fu, Yogatama, Neiswanger (2024) DeLLMa: Decision Making Under Uncertainty with LLMs
finding: An agent loop that does explicit utility elicitation and expected-utility maximisation beats direct prompting, self-consistency and CoT.
numbers: Up to 40% accuracy gain over competing methods in agriculture and stock tasks, with GPT-4, Claude 3, Gemini 1.5. Utility elicited by ranking minibatches, converted to pairwise preferences. Human-LLM ranking agreement 77.5%, similar to human-human.
limits: Tasks built from USDA reports and stock prices.
agent_relevance: Template for a loop: enumerate states, forecast, elicit utility, maximise expected utility.

source: Liu, Fu, Yogatama, Neiswanger (2024) DeLLMa: Decision Making Under Uncertainty with LLMs
finding: Accuracy improves with more test-time compute spent on utility elicitation, and state-forecast calibration tracks overall accuracy.
numbers: Calibration table: GPT-4 0.062, Claude 3 0.142, Gemini 1.5 0.064 (lower is better).
limits: Few models, one calibration metric.
agent_relevance: Spend compute on utility ranking and state forecasting, not only chain-of-thought.

source: Kim, Kovach, Lee, Shin, Tzavellas (2026) Can an LLM Learn Preferences from Choice Data?
finding: LLMs infer a decision maker's risk preferences from observed choices, improving with more observations, unevenly across models.
numbers: GPT learns risk aversion better than disappointment aversion; Gemini best in high disappointment-aversion regions; Claude broadest. 5 observations are enough to reproduce a corner-solution pattern.
limits: Simulated decision makers with known parameters.
agent_relevance: A model can learn a user's value scale from a few choices, useful for personalisation.

source: Horton (2023/2025) Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
finding: LLM agents given preferences reproduce several classic economic results: fairness limits on price gouging (Kahneman et al. 1986), status quo bias, and a minimum-wage hiring shift.
numbers: Original human result: about 82% judged the price rise unfair. Status-quo bias strong in some LLMs, almost absent in others.
limits: Qualitative replication; model-dependent.
agent_relevance: LLM simulations are cheap probes of value structure.

source: Coletta et al. (2024) LLM-driven Imitation of Subrational Behavior: Illusion or Reality?
finding: GPT-4 synthetic demonstrations trained RL agents with prospect-theory behaviour (risk averse in gains, risk seeking in losses) in a double-or-nothing gamble.
numbers: Qualitative replication; also ultimatum game and marshmallow test; 10 synthetic observations.
limits: Small illustrative scenarios.
agent_relevance: Not evidence that the model itself has value; shows an LLM as a source of simulated valuation.

source: Han, Lim, Kong, Jo (2025/2026) Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression: Intrinsic vs. Prompted Values in LLMs
finding: Value expression from training and from prompting rely on partly distinct mechanisms. Value vectors steer behaviour; prompted vectors are more steerable.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; steering strength 4.0, middle layers best; effect grows roughly linearly with strength. Steering with intrinsic-orthogonal directions keeps effect after removing 32-73% of the norm.
limits: Values are Schwartz human values, not reward value.
agent_relevance: Prompted and trained values are not one common scale.

source: Spiegel et al. (2025) Pre-trained Language Models Learn Remarkably Accurate Representations of Numbers
finding: Abstract only: earlier probes failed to read exact numeric values from LMs, the authors argue because probes did not fit the learned structure.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Not read in full. Magnitude, not subjective value.
agent_relevance: A common numeric scale may exist in embeddings.
